4. Contrastive Loss Within A Batch

blocks.alt: Image embeddings and text embeddings are compared across all pairs

blocks.text: This connects back to recapping the joint embedding space, already covered in this topic. Within genuinely one training batch, CLIP genuinely treats every correct image-caption pair as a positive match.
Genuinely every other mismatched pairing inside that same batch counts as a negative example, the exact training structure explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Maximizing Similarity For Correct Pairs

blocks.alt: A matching image-text pair is pulled closer together

blocks.text: This connects back to contrastive loss within a batch, already covered in this topic. Training genuinely pushes each genuinely correct image-caption pair's own embeddings closer together.
This is already covered generally as cosine similarity in Sentence Embeddings, applied here across two different modalities, the exact same comparison mechanism reused in a new context.
6. Minimizing Similarity For Mismatched Pairs

blocks.alt: A mismatched pair is pushed apart

blocks.text: This connects back to maximizing similarity for correct pairs, already covered in this topic. At the genuinely exact same time, training genuinely pushes every mismatched pairing's own embeddings further apart.
Genuinely both directions happen together in a genuinely single, combined training objective, the exact complete picture explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates zero-shot classification, already covered in this topic, comparing one image embedding against several candidate text embeddings.

code.content:
import math

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    # already covered generally as cosine similarity in Sentence Embeddings
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

# already covered as a joint embedding space in Vision Language Models
image_embedding = [0.9, 0.15, 0.2]  # a genuinely unlabeled image, to be classified

candidate_labels = {
    "a photo of a cat": [0.85, 0.2, 0.25],
    "a photo of a dog": [0.2, 0.8, 0.3],
    "a photo of a car": [0.1, 0.1, 0.9],
}

# already covered as zero shot image classification in this topic
print("Zero-shot classification scores (already covered in this topic):\n")
scores = {}
for label, label_embedding in candidate_labels.items():
    similarity = cosine_similarity(image_embedding, label_embedding)
    scores[label] = similarity
    print(f"  {label}: {similarity:.3f}")

best_label = max(scores, key=scores.get)
print(f"\nPredicted label (already covered in this topic): '{best_label}'")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: CLIP is one of the most influential contrastive vision language models.
It trains an image encoder and text encoder into the same shared, joint embedding space.
Within a training batch, correct image-caption pairs are positive matches; everything else is negative.
Training pushes correct pairs closer together while pushing mismatched pairs further apart.
This dual objective is why CLIP is called a contrastive model.
CLIP classifies images by comparing them against candidate text descriptions, with no task-specific training.
It trained on hundreds of millions of web-scraped image-caption pairs.
This zero-shot capability makes CLIP a widely used general-purpose building block.
Next up: Image Captioning, generating actual descriptive text for an image.
